chief_complaint: progressive breathlessness on exertion, chronic dry cough, and spontaneous lung collapses for 2 years
hpi_details: 2-year history of insidious, progressively worsening shortness of breath when walking uphill or exercising, accompanied by a persistent dry cough. Over the past 18 months, she has suffered two separate episodes of spontaneous pneumothorax (collapsed lung) affecting her right and left lungs, requiring chest tube drainage. Has noticed small, skin-coloured papules across her face and cheeks (angiofibromas) since her early twenties, and suffered an episode of flank pain last year caused by a benign kidney tumour (angiomyolipoma). Denies ever smoking cigarettes or working with industrial chemicals.
ideas: thinks her underlying genetic skin and kidney condition has now spread to create delicate cysts inside her lung tissue
concerns: terrified she will require a double lung transplant or die young from respiratory failure
expectations: wants specific high-resolution CT lung scans and targeted mTOR inhibitor medication to halt the cyst formation
pmh: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC -> facial angiofibromas, renal angiomyolipoma), two spontaneous pneumothoraces
social_hx: never smoked, zero alcohol, graphic designer, single

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM -> Tuberous Sclerosis-associated LAM / TSC-LAM, a rare neoplastic proliferation of smooth muscle-like cells exclusively affecting females of childbearing age) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Specialist referral to a designated rare lung disease / LAM center, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive breathlessness on exertion, chronic dry cough, and spontaneous lung collapses for 2 years

Key HPI features: 2-year history of insidious, progressively worsening shortness of breath when walking uphill or exercising, accompanied by a persistent dry cough. Over the past 18 months, she has suffered two separate episodes of spontaneous pneumothorax (collapsed lung) affecting her right and left lungs, requiring chest tube drainage. Has noticed small, skin-coloured papules across her face and cheeks (angiofibromas) since her early twenties, and suffered an episode of flank pain last year caused by a benign kidney tumour (angiomyolipoma). Denies ever smoking cigarettes or working with industrial chemicals.

Objective/Exam findings: Perform targeted physical and dermatological examination. Skin: multiple facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) over cheeks and nose, ash-leaf hypopigmented macules, and shagreen patch over lower back confirming Tuberous Sclerosis. Chest auscultation: vesicular breath sounds, with or without diminished air entry if residual pneumothorax exists. Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs): demonstrates Obstructive or Mixed Obstructive/Restrictive pattern with air trapping (elevated Residual Volume / TLC) and markedly reduced DLCO ( pathognomonic findings): reveals diffuse, bilateral, thin-walled, round, uniform lung cysts distributed evenly throughout all lung zones (costophrenic angles included) with completely normal intervening lung parenchyma and absence of nodules. Serum biomarkers: check Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor D (VEGF-D -> serum level >800 pg/mL is diagnostic of LAM, eliminating the need for open lung biopsy). Check abdominal MRI to monitor bilateral renal angiomyolipomas.
Relevant background/PMH: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC -> facial angiofibromas, renal angiomyolipoma), two spontaneous pneumothoraces
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM -> Tuberous Sclerosis-associated LAM / TSC-LAM, a rare neoplastic proliferation of smooth muscle-like cells exclusively affecting females of childbearing age).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Community-acquired pneumonia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90%).
management_principles: Specialist referral to a designated rare lung disease / LAM center
A LAM specialist may consider sirolimus after confirming indications, contraindications, and a monitoring plan.
Recurrent pneumothorax requires urgent assessment and specialist discussion of recurrence-prevention options.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 31F with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex presents with 2-year progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, and recurrent bilateral spontaneous pneumothoraces.
reference_soap.objective: Perform targeted physical and dermatological examination. Skin: multiple facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) over cheeks and nose, ash-leaf hypopigmented macules, and shagreen patch over lower back confirming Tuberous Sclerosis. Chest auscultation: vesicular breath sounds, with or without diminished air entry if residual pneumothorax exists. Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs): demonstrates Obstructive or Mixed Obstructive/Restrictive pattern with air trapping (elevated Residual Volume / TLC) and markedly reduced DLCO (<50% predicted). High-Resolution CT (HRCT) Chest (thin-section non-contrast -> pathognomonic findings): reveals diffuse, bilateral, thin-walled, round, uniform lung cysts distributed evenly throughout all lung zones (costophrenic angles included) with completely normal intervening lung parenchyma and absence of nodules. Serum biomarkers: check Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor D (VEGF-D -> serum level >800 pg/mL is diagnostic of LAM, eliminating the need for open lung biopsy). Check abdominal MRI to monitor bilateral renal angiomyolipomas.
reference_soap.assessment: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM -> Tuberous Sclerosis-associated LAM / TSC-LAM, a rare neoplastic proliferation of smooth muscle-like cells exclusively affecting females of childbearing age). DDx: Pulmonary Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (PLCH -> occurs in heavy smokers, shows bizarre irregular stellate cysts sparing costophrenic angles), Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (basal lentiform cysts with renal chromophobe carcinomas), severe emphysema.
reference_soap.plan: Refer to a specialist LAM/rare-lung-disease service for diagnostic confirmation, lung-function follow-up, renal surveillance, and reproductive counselling. A specialist may consider sirolimus for appropriate disease severity after reviewing contraindications, interactions, pregnancy plans, and monitoring requirements. New sudden chest pain or breathlessness needs emergency assessment for pneumothorax. Discuss recurrence-prevention procedures and contraception/pregnancy decisions individually with the specialist team; consider transplant referral only for advanced disease after multidisciplinary assessment.

learning_objectives: Correlate Tuberous Sclerosis stigmata (angiofibromas, angiomyolipomas) and recurrent pneumothoraces in women with Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
Interpret HRCT showing diffuse, uniform, thin-walled bilateral lung cysts and elevate serum VEGF-D (>800 pg/mL) as diagnostic
Recognize when a LAM specialist may consider mTOR inhibition with monitoring
Explain the need for individualized reproductive counselling and specialist management of recurrent pneumothorax

teaching.one_liner: Progressive dyspnoea with recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces and TSC features suggests cystic lung disease from LAM.
red_flags: Sudden pleuritic chest pain or worsening breathlessness suggesting pneumothorax

must_ask.say: You've had two collapsed lungs - can you tell me when each happened and how they were treated?

must_ask.objective: Renal angiomyolipoma and flank pain symptoms
must_ask.say: Have you had any flank or abdominal pain, or been told about a kidney growth?

must_ask.objective: Tuberous sclerosis stigmata and family history
must_ask.say: Have you noticed small facial skin bumps since your twenties, or does anyone in your family have tuberous sclerosis?

must_ask.objective: Hormonal factors: sex, age, menstrual and pregnancy history
must_ask.say: Does your breathlessness change around your menstrual cycle, and have you ever been pregnant?
How far can you walk now compared to two years ago before you get breathless?
